hook: A weather station logs temperature, its rate of change, and how fast that rate is changing. A forecaster reading the three together can say "still warming, but the warming is easing off, so the high is coming soon." Reading $f$, $f'$ and $f''$ together is the same skill, and the graph-of-$f'$ question on the exam is built on it.

figure.caption: Three graphs on one $x$-axis. Where $f$ peaks, $f'$ is zero; where $f$ inflects, $f'$ is at an extreme and $f''$ is zero; where $f''$ is negative, $f$ is concave down.

ideas: Graphical analysis: given any one of $f$, $f'$, $f''$ (graph, table or formula), read the features of the others.
From a graph of $f'$: sign of $f'$ (above or below the axis) gives increasing or decreasing; direction of $f'$ (rising or falling) gives concavity.

From a table: $f'(a) = 0$ and the sign of $f''(a)$ give the Second Derivative Test; a continuous $f''$ that changes from positive to negative between two inputs gives a point of inflection between them.
Words: "increasing at a decreasing rate" means $f' > 0$ and $f'' < 0$.

misconception.wrong: On a graph of $f'$, the points of inflection of $f$ are where the graph of $f'$ crosses the $x$-axis.
misconception.right: Crossings of $f'$ are where $f$ has extrema. Inflection points of $f$ are where $f'$ turns (its peaks and valleys), because that is where $f''$ changes sign. Chief readers see this swap every year.

summary: The three graphs carry one story. $f'$ gives the direction of $f$, and its sign changes give extrema. $f''$ (or whether $f'$ rises or falls) gives the concavity of $f$, and its sign changes give inflection points. Read from whichever representation you have, and name the function in every justification.
